article.title: What I'll Be Watching
article.author: John Peeler
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On the brink of the 2026 midterms, it’s time for clear thinking about what to expect. Moreover, the drama won’t end on election night. Vote counting in numerous close elections will be contested as the Trump administration calls into question any close results that go against Republicans. And even the timely swearing-in of the new Congress cannot be taken for granted as the outgoing majority may try to block some or all newly elected Democrats. First, the straight-up election results. All indicators point to a very good day for the Democrats as independent voters swing decisively to the Democrats, reacting to escalating cost of living, especially fuel prices, largely due to the very unpopular and seemingly interminable war with Iran. The voters are also giving more prominence to the issue of rampant corruption in the Trump administration and the Trump family. The Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives, perhaps with a swing of 15 to 20 seats. To take the Senate they would have to net four or more seats. It looks like they can hold Georgia, New Hampshire and Minnesota, and are expected to take North Carolina. They will need to hold Michigan, and pick up three of more Republican seats off a list that would have seemed impossible a few months ago. Related: Polls in the Hole? How Much Hope Has the GOP? Eight GOP-held seats are in play: Maine, Ohio, South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Texas, Alaska and Nebraska. I think the most likely Democratic wins will be in Maine, Ohio, Texas, Alaska and Kansas. Those will suffice for a Democratic majority, if the party can hold on to all the seats it has. Any additional wins will expand the majority, but there’s no way they’ll get to a filibuster-proof 60 votes. Having recently moved from the swing state of Pennsylvania to solidly Democratic Massachusetts, I will be watching these two states closely. In Pennsylvania, Governor Shapiro is overwhelmingly popular and likely to do well even in Republican areas. In Massachusetts, Governor Maura Healey is not so highly regarded, but will likely easily win reelection anyway. I’ll be watching four GOP-held House seats in Pennsylvania: if the Democrats sweep all four they will be set for a very good night. I’ll also be watching the margins in Republican areas of both states. Given the national climate so favorable to Democrats, I’d expect Republican vote totals to be down, but the GOP will probably still win those areas in Pennsylvania (but not in Massachusetts, where it’s hard to find any substantial territory with a Republican majority). Thus the Democrats are likely to come out of Election Night with a very substantial national victory. What will happen then? For perhaps a week after election night, we could see several controversies and possibly court cases about election disputes. These may grow out of the presence of federal election observers in selected swing districts around the country. We’ll have to rely primarily on the federal courts to sort them out, with state election officials defending the integrity of their results against the federal effort to cast doubt on them. For the two months from Election Day to the swearing in of the new Congress, I expect a significant number of court challenges from the Trump Department of Justice, in states and districts where Republicans lost narrowly. Many defenders of democracy are convinced that Trump will mount a full-court press nationwide to undo the election results. That’s possible, but I don’t think it’s likely. I don’t think Trump has the self-discipline to pull something like that. Sowing chaos is more his style. Related: Receivership: Agenda for a Democratic Congress Speaker Mike Johnson could appoint a House Clerk willing to withhold recognition for some or all elected Democratic members of Congress. Johnson won’t have enough control over his paper-thin, exit-bound majority to pull it off successfully. But it would pose a major constitutional crisis that would merit millions of voters in the streets nationwide. After Congress is sworn in, expect multiple investigations and conflicts over appropriations through the 2028 presidential election. Trump will likely become even more authoritarian, evermore defiant against both legislative and judicial restraints. Buckle up!
